title: 'Rom-Coms Started and Ended With Me': Saif Ali Khan Says the Genre Was a Beautiful Failed Experiment
excerpt: The actor who defined NRI romance in Hum Tum and Salaam Namaste says audiences no longer connect with the 'confused privileged guy' — and his wife agrees
body:
There was a time — roughly 2004 to 2008 — when a very specific kind of Bollywood film dominated NRI living rooms. The hero was urban, witty, slightly confused about life despite having everything going for him. The heroine was independent, sharp-tongued, and destined to fall for him anyway. The setting was always somewhere photogenic: Amsterdam, Melbourne, New York. And the leading man, more often than not, was **Saif Ali Khan**.

Now, riding the success of his crime drama *Kartavya* (which premiered on an OTT platform on May 15, produced by Shah Rukh Khan and Gauri Khan's Red Chillies Entertainment), Saif has delivered what might be the most honest epitaph for a genre he personally defined.

"I loved doing romcoms, but I feel they were like an anomaly in Indian cinema which might have even started and finished with me in a sense," he told HT City. "I think rom-coms are a failed experiment, although a beautiful one."

## The Genre That Spoke to NRIs

For diaspora audiences, Saif's rom-com era wasn't just entertainment — it was representation. *Hum Tum* (2004) earned him a National Film Award and gave NRIs a Bollywood hero who felt recognizably modern: someone who read books, cracked jokes that actually landed, and navigated relationships with the same messy uncertainty that second-generation Indians experienced daily.

*Salaam Namaste* (2005) went further, setting its entire story in Melbourne and tackling live-in relationships and unplanned pregnancy — subjects that mainstream Bollywood had barely acknowledged. For Indian families in Australia, the UK, and North America, these weren't just films. They were the first time Bollywood seemed to understand that NRI life wasn't all airport reunions and melodramatic homecomings.

## Why It Failed (According to Saif)

Saif's diagnosis is characteristically blunt. "A rom-com is technically this confused privileged guy who has everything on his plate but is still confused, so people don't really connect with it now," he explained. "They wonder what is his problem. So, firstly, things are not that bad, and secondly, it is something you shouldn't do after a certain age."

It's a sharp reading of how Indian audiences have changed. The aspirational urban lifestyle that rom-coms sold — the overseas holidays, the coffee shop conversations, the beautiful apartments — no longer feels aspirational when a significant chunk of the audience actually lives that life. NRIs who once saw these films as mirrors now see them as slightly dated fantasies.

**Kareena Kapoor Khan**, Saif's wife, apparently agrees — with a twist. "My wife said to me that things must be sorted now in your head; you can't be playing this confused man," Saif shared. "Ibrahim should do more of it now; it's our family business." The suggestion that son **Ibrahim Ali Khan**, who recently entered acting, might inherit the rom-com crown is both funny and pointed: the genre needs youth, not wisdom, to work.

## The Deeper Desire

But Saif isn't entirely ready to close the chapter. "There is something going deeper in Indian society, which is the want for a love story," he reflected. "I would love to do a love story, or even a comedy that ends in romance. Now, I feel I can do another romcom, there is still one there in me."

This distinction — between a rom-com (genre formula) and a love story (human need) — is worth pausing on. Indian cinema's biggest recent successes have included romantic elements without being rom-coms: *Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani* worked because it was a family drama wrapped in romance, not a pure rom-com. *Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar* tried the classic formula and underperformed relative to expectations.

## What NRIs Lost When Rom-Coms Died

The disappearance of the Bollywood rom-com leaves a specific gap for diaspora audiences. These were films you could watch with your parents without cringing, recommend to non-Indian friends without lengthy cultural footnotes, and genuinely enjoy without the three-hour commitment of an epic. They were Bollywood's most exportable product.

Today, the space they occupied has been filled by OTT thrillers, action franchises, and social dramas. All worthy. But none with the easy, breezy charm of watching Saif Ali Khan fumble his way through falling in love in a European city.

*Kartavya* is now streaming, produced by Red Chillies Entertainment. Ibrahim Ali Khan's career trajectory remains to be seen — but if Kareena Kapoor Khan has her way, the family business of rom-coms might yet find a successor.
